tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark timings in the README (bench/run.cpp, which times delaunator-cpp only) with no compiler, no CPU model and a JS-only baseline whose ~10% figure lives in PR #8; a third-party table in the Delaunay32 README (competitor-run, compiler and flags not stated) adds Triangle/CDT numbers but is not a well-known independent suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Probably the fastest C++ open source 2D Delaunay implementation' and 'Library is ~10% faster then JS version for 1M uniform points' (links PR #8). Own Google Benchmark run dated 2018-09-29: 45K geojson nodes 22 ms; 2,000 uniform points 1 ms; 100,000 63 ms; 200,000 140 ms; 500,000 400 ms; 1,000,000 994 ms. In PR #8 the author's first claim, 'Roughly 6 times faster then JS version', was challenged by mourner (benchmarks showed ~20-30%; the JS script had no JIT warmup); after both benchmarks were reworked the author reported ~30 ms of JS overhead on small inputs and a ~10% difference at 1M points. Third-party: the Delaunay32 README table (1M unique integer points, Apple M1, 1 thread, triangle-only output) lists delaunator-cpp c1521f6 at 542.0 ms vs Triangle 1.6 at 584.0 ms and CDT 1.4.5 at 988.7 ms, i.e. about 1.08x faster than Triangle and 1.8x faster than CDT, but 4.1x slower than single-thread Delaunay32 (131.6 ms) and 1.7x slower than single-thread Fade2D 2.17.3 (314.1 ms) (ratios derived from page data).
corrections.baseline: mapbox/delaunator (JavaScript original), in its own README and PR #8; the repo has no C++ baseline (bench/run.cpp times delaunator-cpp only). A third-party table in the Delaunay32 README compares it with Triangle 1.6, CDT 1.4.5 and Fade2D 2.17.3.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README run; CMakeLists.txt release build sets -O3 -DNDEBUG with C++14 (compiler unspecified).
corrections.caveats: Its own evidence compares only against the JS original of the same algorithm (~10% at 1M points after the 6x claim was retracted in PR #8); bench/run.cpp benchmarks delaunator-cpp alone, and CGAL, Triangle and poly2tri are never measured in the repo (issue #34 'Comparison with CGAL?' got no numbers). Numbers are first-party from 2018 with no compiler and no CPU model ('4 X 2300 MHz CPU'). The only C++ comparison is a competitor's table (Delaunay32 README, Apple M1, compiler and flags not stated): delaunator-cpp is about 1.08x faster than Triangle 1.6 but 4.1x slower than single-thread Delaunay32 and 1.7x slower than single-thread Fade2D, which contradicts the hedged 'probably the fastest' claim; Delaunay32 is already catalogued. Correctness: open issue #16 reports an infinite loop in legalize() on a 136-point input (opened 2019-04-19 and still open; the issue page links PR #32 as a proposed fix), and the open-issue list also has 'Division by zero when finding third point', 'orient function robustness issue' and 'Unsigned integer overflow detected by AddressSanitizer'; predicates are plain floating point. Abandoned since 2018-10-07.

notes: Measures itself only against the JS original (delaunator), not against CGAL, Triangle or poly2tri; a C++ comparison exists only in the third-party Delaunay32 README (barely ahead of Triangle, well behind Delaunay32 and Fade2D). Record the open infinite-loop and division-by-zero issues as correctness shortcomings. The HN-snippet figures in the input caveats were replaced with the Delaunay32 README numbers I opened.

tier_reason: First-party: the benchmark code is public (test/bench.cpp BM_EarcutTiles) and the CPU is stated (M1 Pro), but compiler and flags for the 276 ms figure are not, and the README gives the JS comparison only qualitatively (the JS number sits in the earcut.js README), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 119,680 real-world MVT polygons (1.9M vertices, map-tile window at zooms 4-16) triangulated in ~276 ms on a MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021), 'noticeably faster than the JS original'; optional Delaunay refinement adds ~98 ms. The earcut.js README states ~445 ms (refinement ~168 ms) for the same 119,680-polygon set on the same MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021), so earcut.hpp is about 1.6x faster than earcut.js (refinement about 1.7x) (derived from page data across the two READMEs; Node version and C++ compiler/flags not stated).
corrections.baseline: earcut.js, the original JavaScript implementation (~445 ms for the same set in its README); test/bench.cpp also times libtess2 v1.0.2 on 9 small fixtures but publishes no results; CGAL and libtess2 are called 'slower and larger' in the README without numbers.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 276 ms figure; CMakeLists.txt defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with C++17 for the bench and no -march (compiler unspecified).
corrections.caveats: The only quantified baseline is the same-algorithm JS original (about 1.6x, derived across two READMEs on the same machine), a weak result. test/bench.cpp registers BM_LibtessTriangulation (libtess2 v1.0.2 fetched by CMake) only on 9 whitelisted fixtures (building, dude, water, water2, water3, water3b, water4, water_huge, water_huge2); the 119,680-polygon tile benchmark (BM_EarcutTiles) has no libtess2 or other C++ counterpart, and no libtess2 results are published, so the C++ comparison needs a local run. No CGAL, poly2tri or Triangle measurement. Compiler and flags for the 276 ms figure are not stated. By design earcut does not guarantee a correct triangulation: the README says that on invalid input (self-crossing or overlapping rings, holes outside the outer ring, duplicate or zero-length edges) the output can contain overlapping triangles, gaps or triangles outside the polygon; the output is not conforming (T-junctions), and refine() uses non-robust predicates.

notes: Measures its own speed only against the JS original (earcut.js; ~276 vs ~445 ms on the same M1 Pro, ratio derived across READMEs); bench.cpp has an unpublished libtess2 comparison on small fixtures only; no CGAL/Triangle/poly2tri numbers. Metadata checked: ISC, 1.0k stars, last commit 2026-09-28, not a fork.

tier_reason: First-party suite and run (Apache Sedona's own SpatialBench, docs/single-node-benchmarks.md) with public benchmark code, pinned versions and an instance type (m7i.2xlarge) but no CPU model and no build flags, and some gains exceed 50x, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SpatialBench raw table (seconds, SedonaDB / DuckDB / GeoPandas). SF1: q1 0.66/0.96/12.78; q2 8.07/9.95/20.74; q3 0.80/1.17/13.59; q4 8.41/9.83/25.24; q5 5.10/1.80/47.08; q6 8.59/9.36/24.43; q7 1.66/1.82/137.00; q8 1.10/1.08/16.08; q9 0.23/50.15/0.28; q10 18.79/207.84/46.13; q11 32.98/TIMEOUT/51.01; q12 14.55/ERROR/TIMEOUT. SF10: q1 3.04/4.58/ERROR; q2 8.89/8.26/ERROR; q3 4.09/5.17/TIMEOUT; q4 7.52/8.51/ERROR; q5 50.81/14.40/ERROR; q6 9.11/10.67/ERROR; q7 14.44/14.03/ERROR; q8 7.24/7.57/TIMEOUT; q9 0.38/942.98/0.49; q10 42.02/ERROR/ERROR; q11 97.52/ERROR/ERROR; q12 145.66/ERROR/TIMEOUT. Versus DuckDB, SedonaDB is 1.05-1.5x faster on most of q1-q8, about 11x faster on SF1 q10 and 218x (SF1) / 2,480x (SF10) faster on q9, but 2.8x (SF1) and 3.5x (SF10) slower on q5 and marginally slower on SF1 q8 and SF10 q2 and q7. Versus GeoPandas at SF1 it is 1.2x (q9) to 82x (q7) faster on q1-q11 (ratios derived from page data). ERROR/TIMEOUT cells are failures, not ratios. The page itself calls Q5 spatial aggregation a known SedonaDB weakness.
corrections.hardware: AWS EC2 m7i.2xlarge (8 CPUs, 32 GB RAM); CPU model not named on the page
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Released packages with default settings: SedonaDB 0.1.0, DuckDB 1.4.0 (enable_external_file_cache=false), GeoPandas 1.1.1 with Shapely 2.1.1 and NumPy 2.3.3; build flags not stated.
corrections.workload: SpatialBench v0.1.0 pre-release (commit 9094be8) queries 1-12 at scale factors 1 and 10, run 2025-09-22: spatial filters, geometric computations, spatial joins and KNN joins over dbgen-generated Parquet (WKB geometry) read directly from S3; runtime includes data loading, each result is COUNTed, 1200 s timeout; GeoPandas runs a hand-written single-threaded Python mirror of the SQL.
corrections.caveats: First-party: SpatialBench is the Apache Sedona project's own suite and the results page was written by the same project (datasets sit in a 'wherobots-examples' S3 bucket). The numbers are a year old (SedonaDB 0.1.0, run 2025-09-22) and come from one instance type with no CPU model, no build flags and no stated run count. Baselines are other spatial engines (DuckDB 1.4.0 spatial, GeoPandas 1.1.1/Shapely 2.1.1), not GEOS/CGAL/Boost.Geometry directly. Results are mixed against DuckDB: SedonaDB is 2.8-3.5x slower on q5 and about even on several filter queries; the very large q9/q10 wins and the DuckDB/GeoPandas ERROR and TIMEOUT cells reflect missing native KNN joins or poor plans in the other engines (the page says DuckDB and GeoPandas lack KNN join support and needed hand-written code), not raw geometry speed. GeoPandas is a single-threaded hand-written port. SedonaDB is a Rust engine on DataFusion/Arrow with Python/R bindings, not a C++ library, and is a spatial SQL engine rather than a geometry kernel.

notes: The README charts point to sedona.apache.org (blocked), but the same results page is checked into apache/sedona-spatialbench docs/single-node-benchmarks.md with an exact raw table, hardware (m7i.2xlarge) and versions; benchmark_url corrected to it and bar readings replaced with the table values. Off-language (Rust) and arguably a database engine rather than a geometry library; record as shortcoming.
